en: The Sūtra on the Arising of the Bodhicitta and the Destruction of All Māras, Spoken by the Buddha, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperial Court Attendant,
Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, Recipient of the Purple Robe.
Translated by the Subject Shi Hu by Imperial Decree. Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, as well as a multitude of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all gathered there.

At that time, there lived in the great city of Rājagṛha a great Brahmin of the Kāśyapa clan. One night, he suddenly saw in a dream this Jambudvīpa world as a vast lotus flower with a thousand petals, adorned with the seven precious jewels, pure and lovely. Within that flower was a great lunar disc, immacinate and full, its surrounding radiance blazing and shining intensely.
That brahmin beheld these signs within his dream; his heart was filled with great joy, delight, and exultation.
Upon waking from the dream, he reflected:

"I have heard that the śramaṇa Gautama is a man of great wisdom, whom no other wise person can surpass, and who is fully endowed with skillful means and great intelligence. I should go to him and inquire about these signs."

Having formed this thought, the brahmin passed the night and at dawn went to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery. Upon arrival, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One, joined his palms in reverence, and reported in detail to the Buddha everything he had seen in his dream.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the brahmin, saying:
"The dream you have had is an auspicious omen, O brahmin!"
You should now know that if a person sees four kinds of signs in a dream, they are all the most supreme and auspicious of signs.
What are these four?
The first is a white lotus flower.
Second, the white parasol;
third, the lunar disc;
fourth, the image of the Buddha.
"If one sees these four kinds of signs, know that one will certainly attain the most supreme and great benefit.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"If one sees the sign of a lotus flower in a dream, And a white parasol, both are auspicious;
If one sees a pure, great lunar disc, the dreamer shall obtain the most supreme benefit.
Furthermore, if one sees the image of a Buddha, this sign is the most excellent among the excellent;
such a person will be loved and respected by all, and shall be able to accomplish all meritorious virtues.
At that time, the brahmin again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is called the supreme and greatest benefit?”
“For what reason did the Buddha speak thus?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the brāhmaṇa with a verse:
“I shall now explain that great benefit; you, O brāhmaṇa, should listen attentively.”
If a person can give rise to the bodhicitta, they will become a Most Honored Among Two-Legged Beings, known as one of Great Benefit.
Even the status of a Cakravartin King is noble and supreme, ruling over the four great continents with sovereignty;
yet if there are sentient beings who desire to achieve even greater perfection, they should give rise to the bodhicitta.
The Lord Śakra, Sovereign of Devas, enjoys supreme karmic rewards and exercises mastery over the Heaven of the Thirty-three;
if sentient beings desire such accomplishment, they should give rise to the bodhicitta.
Within the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness, each respective karmic reward is increasingly superior;
if there are sentient beings who delight in accomplishment, they should give rise to the bodhicitta.
The realms of all sentient beings are boundless; One should skillfully transform and deliver them as is appropriate.
If one wishes to extensively bring benefit and joy to others, One should give rise to the bodhicitta.
All the great physicians in the world Are able to cure every ailment;
If there are sentient beings who wish for accomplishment, They should give rise to the bodhicitta.
Manifesting great radiance throughout the world, It illuminates all darkness and obscurity;
If there are sentient beings who desire accomplishment, They should give rise to the bodhicitta.
Though one may be born within the three realms, one should sever all inverted practices;
if there are sentient beings who delight in renunciation, they should give rise to the bodhicitta.
All afflictions and various obstacles, as well as all other unwholesome dharmas—
if there are sentient beings who wish to sever and eliminate them, they should give rise to the bodhicitta.
All fetters and afflictions within the three realms, Are captured by Māra according to one's actions;
If there are sentient beings who delight in severing them, They should give rise to the bodhicitta.
If one can subdue ignorance, one will be able to sever all nets of craving;
if there are sentient beings who delight in renunciation, they should give rise to the bodhicitta.
If that dharma of craving is severed, all defilements will be purified;
if there are sentient beings who delight in renunciation, they should give rise to the bodhicitta.
Fools harbor arrogance based on their lineage, appearance, and strength;
if there are sentient beings who delight in severing [such pride], they should give rise to the bodhicitta.
Fools cling to the view of a self and the view of a life-span, giving rise to arrogance regarding their own welfare;
if there are sentient beings who delight in eradication and severance, one should arouse the bodhicitta toward them.
One gives rise to arrogance toward all material phenomena; from defiled attachment, great faults arise.
If there are sentient beings who delight in severing these [faults], they should give rise to the bodhicitta.
The foolish rely on extensive learning, observance of precepts, and spiritual practice to give rise to arrogance;
if there are sentient beings who delight in eradication and severance, they should instead give rise to the bodhicitta.
Dwelling in an araṇya and practicing alms-gathering, one might give rise to arrogance regarding such matters;
if there are sentient beings who delight in severing [defilements], they should resolve to generate the bodhicitta.
The Arhats, masters endowed with supernormal powers, Relying on their own nobility and excellence, give rise to arrogance;
If there are sentient beings who delight in severing [these defilements], They should resolve to generate the bodhicitta.
Fools are attached to the signs of self and person, and relying on those notions of self and other, they give rise to arrogance;
if there are sentient beings who delight in severing [these attachments], they should resolve to awaken the bodhicitta.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the present and the future—
by honoring and revering them, one obtains merit;
if there are sentient beings who delight in such benefit, they should give rise to the bodhicitta.
When the Buddhas appear in the world, they turn the great wheel of Dharma to universally transform and deliver beings;
if there are sentient beings who delight in hearing and receiving it, they should give rise to the bodhicitta.
All unwholesome dharmas are to be abandoned; all wholesome dharmas are to be cultivated.
If there are sentient beings who delight in accomplishment, they should give rise to the bodhicitta.
All those who practice the path cultivate the holy life, and through this they realize the untainted way;
if there are sentient beings who delight in accomplishment, they should give rise to the bodhicitta.
The Dharma of impermanence that I have proclaimed— Each and every one should observe it within their own body;
If there are sentient beings who delight in understanding it, They should give rise to the bodhicitta.
I say that all contaminated conditioned phenomena are suffering; the wise, seeing this suffering, give rise to revulsion.
If there are sentient beings who delight in renunciation, they should give rise to the bodhicitta.
I have extensively proclaimed for the sake of sentient beings: One should know that all phenomena are without self;
If there are beings who delight in thorough realization, They should give rise to the bodhicitta.
He proclaims the Dharma of the peace of nirvāṇa, And realizes the unsurpassed, great bodhi;
If there are sentient beings who desire to achieve this, They should give rise to the bodhicitta.
I have praised the bodhicitta; you, O brāhmaṇa, listen with reverence.
If, upon hearing it, you can develop this mind with deep faith, you shall be called a practitioner of bodhi.
At that time, having heard the Buddha proclaim these verses, the brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there is a person who gives rise to the bodhicitta, how much of an accumulation of merit will that person obtain?”
At that time, the World-Honored One again answered the brahmin with a verse:

"Even if all classes of sentient beings were to gather together throughout this entire Buddha-world, and each one were to practice the conduct of pure precepts, fully abiding in the stage of training in the precepts; "
Yet that mass of merit is boundless; among all merits it is the most supreme.
If a person can give rise to the bodhicitta, [all other merit] does not equal even one-sixteenth part of it.
Even if all classes of sentient beings were to gather together throughout this entire Buddha-world,
and each were to give rise to pure faith and abide securely on the stage of practice through faith—
their mass of merit would be boundless, the most supreme among all merits.
If a person can give rise to the bodhicitta, it would not equal even one-sixteenth part [of the merit of such a person].
Even if all classes of sentient beings were to gather together throughout this entire Buddha-world,
each practicing the sublime Dharma-gates and all being able to dwell securely on the stage of Dharma-practice, [it would still not equal the merit of one who has given rise to the bodhicitta].
The measure of that mass of merit is boundless; it is the most supreme among all merits.
If a person can give rise to the bodhicitta, [all other merit] does not equal even one-sixteenth part of it.

Even if all classes of sentient beings were to gather together within this Buddha-world and extensively cultivate the practices of a stream-enterer, such that they all abide in the fruit of a stream-enterer—
the measure of their mass of merit would be boundless, and it would be the most supreme among all merits.
If a person can give rise to the bodhicitta, it would not equal even one-sixteenth part [of the merit of that person].
Even if all classes of sentient beings were to gather together throughout this Buddha-world,
extensively cultivate the practices of the Sakṛdāgāmin, and all dwell in the stage of the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin—
Yet that mass of merit is immeasurable; among all merits it is the most supreme.
If a person can give rise to the bodhicitta, [all other merit] does not equal even one-sixteenth part of it.
Even if all classes of sentient beings were to gather together within this Buddha-world,
universally cultivating the practices for the stage of Anāgāmin and all attaining the fruit of Anāgāmin—
though the measure of their mass of merit were boundless and supreme among all merits— [it would not equal a fraction of the merit of one who hears this Dharma].
If a person can give rise to the bodhicitta, it would not equal even one-sixteenth part [of the merit of such a person].
Even if all classes of sentient beings were to gather together throughout this Buddha-world,
extensively cultivate the practices of an arhat, and all come to abide in the fruit-stage of an arhat—
Yet that mass of merit is immeasurable; among all merits it is the most supreme.
If a person can give rise to the bodhicitta, [all other merit] does not equal even one-sixteenth part of it.
If a person in this Buddha-world were to gather vast quantities of the finest,
most exquisite sandalwood to construct a Buddha-stūpa or temple of supreme adornment, as high and wide as Mount Sumeru,
the mass of merit from such an act would likewise be boundless; among all merits, it is the most preeminent.
If a person can give rise to the bodhicitta, it would not equal even one-sixteenth part [of the merit of such a mind].
Furthermore, if one were to construct various stupas for the Buddhas,
performing them according to the prescribed proportions and extensively adorning them as they are made— this is the supreme karmic fruit for all such sentient beings.
Yet that merit and benefit are vast and boundless, the most supreme among all blessings;
if a person can give rise to the bodhicitta, it cannot be matched by even a sixteenth part of it.
Furthermore, if all classes of sentient beings were to live for the full duration of an eon,
and were to bestow upon other beings every kind of article of pleasure, fulfilling their wishes according to their inclinations—
the mass of merit from such deeds would be boundless; yet among all forms of merit, this is the most supreme.
If a person can give rise to the bodhicitta, it would not equal even one-sixteenth part [of my merit].
All that I have thus proclaimed are each the most supreme dharmas;
if there are sentient beings who take joy in them, they should seek the fruit of the tranquility of bodhi.
Those who abide in this fruit attain great benefit—peerless, unequaled, and most supreme.
Therefore, if anyone hears this Dharma, they should honor it and practice with right wisdom.
"One who extensively cultivates such an accumulation of merit will swiftly realize unsurpassed, great bodhi.
At that time, having heard the Buddha, the World-Honored One, thus praise the bodhicitta, the brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"In the mind of awakening, I have not the slightest dharma that can be turned.
The Buddha told the brahmin: "So it is, so it is!"
"O Brahmin! If a person gives rise to the bodhicitta, in reality there is no dharma that can be turned. Why is this?"
"O Brahmin! You should know that there are three kinds of bodhi.
What are these three?"
They are: the enlightenment of the śrāvaka, the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddha, and unsurpassed enlightenment.
Among these, what is called the enlightenment of the śrāvaka?

“Brahmin! Suppose there is someone who, although they have resolved upon bodhicitta, delights only in their own benefit and does not delight in benefiting others; who is unable to arouse, cultivate, enter into, or abide in the mind that benefits others; who does not delight in hearing or receiving this Dharma of the sutra, nor is able to proclaim it for others; who, in future lives, does not take on a body and cuts off the perception of coming and going, yet is unable to attain impartial, right knowledge; and who, in the present life, seeks only liberation.”
"Brahmin! For this reason, it is called the enlightenment of the śrāvaka.
Furthermore, what is called the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddha?"

This refers to those who, although they have generated the bodhicitta, take no pleasure in practicing the Mahāyāna teachings and do not retain them in mind; furthermore, they seek only their own benefit and the realization of the fruit, taking no pleasure in benefiting others. They are unable to cultivate, enter, or abide in the altruistic mind; they take no pleasure in hearing or receiving this Dharma of the sutra, nor do they proclaim or instruct it for others. Unable to abide in equanimous right wisdom, they merely give rise to thoughts that contemplate all conditioned phenomena (*pratyaya-dharma*), attaining liberation according to what they thus observe.
"Brahmin! For this reason, it is called the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, what is called 'unsurpassed enlightenment'?"

This refers to a person who, having personally generated the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, further exhorts others to generate such a mind; who, having themselves heard, received, practiced, and memorized this Dharma of the sutra, extensively explains its meaning to others; who does not give rise to weariness regarding the body within saṃsāra; who desires to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings; who, having attained liberation for themselves by abiding in the wisdom of equality, desires to cause all sentient beings to likewise attain liberation; and who, having achieved their own welfare and the welfare of others to obtain peaceful bliss, universally bestows their own virtuous benefits upon the entire assembly of devas and humans.
Brahmin! For this reason, it is called unsurpassed bodhi;
those who cultivate this practice are called followers of the Bodhisattva Vehicle.

“Brāhmaṇa! You should now know that the words of the Buddha are truthful and sincere, without any falsehood. As I have taught, the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is the supreme meaning; if one departs from this great bodhicitta and instead gives rise to the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, one cannot benefit others and will ultimately fail to reach the realm of Great Nirvāṇa.”

Why is this? Because those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, being intent on their own self-benefit, no longer give rise to the superior practice of benefiting others. For this reason, they are unable to fulfill the factors of the Buddha-dharma; although they may have generated the bodhicitta, they consider themselves liberated, and that bodhicitta cannot yield the fruit of benefiting others.

"O Brāhmaṇa! If a person can resolve their mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they are equal toward both themselves and others; they joyfully practice giving for the benefit of themselves and others, and by means of this very mind, they universally gather in all sentient beings of the world. This constitutes the supreme and greatest benefit for the world, and such a person is also called a 'skillful trainer' of the world."
In this way, one is able to abide in the wisdom of equality, which is supreme, most excellent, and inconceivable.
O Brahmin! This is what is called the Great Bodhicitta; you should understand it thus, according to reality."
At that time, the brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
You speak of liberation; why does it possess various different characteristics?"
The Buddha said:
"Brahmin! The liberation of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and tathāgatas is without various characteristics."

"Brāhmaṇa! It is like a person who, mounting three kinds of animals, wishes to go to a place of jewels; although the paths they tread upon differ according to the vehicle, the destination they head toward is no different."
As for those three animals, they are the donkey, the horse, and the elephant.

That person riding the donkey possesses weak and inferior strength; for this reason, although he reaches the place of treasure, he is unable to extensively bestow those precious jewels upon sentient beings, but instead delights only in self-benefit and attaining nirvāṇa.

That horse-vehicle is light, agile, and swift; by its power, although this person reaches the place of treasures, he is nevertheless unable to extensively bestow those precious jewels upon sentient beings, but merely serves as a pure field of merit for them.

That elephant-vehicle moves with steady, upright gait and possesses great courage and strength; by its power, this person reaches the vast city where all treasures are gathered. Having reached that city, he immediately thinks: "The precious jewels of the three vehicles all emerge from here;
I shall universally bestow these immeasurable precious jewels upon all boundless sentient beings, extensively bringing about their great benefit and happiness."
"O Brahmin! The practitioners of the three vehicles who cultivate the teachings of the three vehicles are also like this.
That which is the donkey vehicle is the Śrāvaka vehicle."
That which is the horse vehicle is the Pratyekabuddha vehicle;
that which is the elephant vehicle is the Mahāyāna.

You should now know that although these three vehicles have various characteristics, the nirvāṇa they realize and the liberation they attain are without various characteristics and without distinction.
“Brahmin! It is as if there were three men in the world who all wished to cross a deep great river.
The first man crossed by relying on a single small leaf floating upon the water;”
That second person surpasses the former, crossing by floating upon a wooden plank;

that third person again surpasses the former, crossing safely to the other shore in a large ship together with a great multitude of people. This is further like the eldest son in the world, who causes his parents to have nothing to guard against and frees them from all sorrows and afflictions in every circumstance.
"Brahmin! You should know that the first person who crosses by relying on leaves is one who belongs to the Śrāvaka-yāna;
you should know that the second person who succeeds in crossing by relying on wooden planks is one who belongs to the Pratyekabuddha-yāna."

Brahmin, you should know that the third person who crosses over by means of a boat is one who belongs to the Bodhisattva vehicle; having attained deliverance for himself, he further delivers others. Brahmin!

Therefore, you should know that although the dharmas practiced by those of the three vehicles possess various characteristics, the nirvāṇa realized by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the Tathāgatas is devoid of various characteristics.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“The three vehicles realize nirvāṇa; It is the same single dharma of nirvāṇa.
Though there are differences in the realization of the Path, Nirvāṇa has no dual characteristics.”
All Buddhas of the three periods of time have attained supreme liberation;
such is the Dharma-eye taught by the Honored One, the Perfectly Awakened One.
This is the supreme wisdom of the Dharma, which gives rise to all skillful means.
"All those who practice should train in this manner.
*The Sūtra on Generating the Bodhicitta and Destroying All Māras*, Volume Upper.
*The Sūtra on Generating the Bodhicitta and Destroying All Māras*, Volume Lower.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīladharma (Shi Hu), Imperially Appointed Grand Master for the Propagation of the Dharma,
Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, and Recipient of the Purple Robe,
during the Song Dynasty. At that time, the Great Brāhmaṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What practice should those who cultivate the Mahāyāna dharma perform?
The Buddha addressed the brahmin, saying:
“As I have now spoken, so should you practice.
O Brahmin! You should know this:

if there are those who cultivate the Mahāyāna Dharma, having themselves resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they further exhort others to resolve their minds likewise, and extensively proclaim and instruct this scriptural Dharma for others—such persons as these should be approached, honored, and revered; such persons universally gather in sentient beings through the four methods of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*).”
What are the four? They are:
giving, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation.
In this context, what is called "generosity"?

It refers to whether the material gift is small or large, one gives rise to a vast mind according to one's own capacity; by means of such giving, one gathers in those who are stingy and greedy. This is called the generosity included within the practice of a Mahāyāna practitioner.
What is called "loving speech"?
It refers to this:

whenever one encounters sentient beings in any place, one should maintain a joyful countenance and speak with gentleness; using various skillful means to comfort them and welcome them, one gathers in those who are coarse and wicked through such loving speech. This is what is meant by the inclusion of loving speech for those practicing the Mahāyāna.
What is called beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*)? It is as follows:

seeing all wholesome dharmas, one practices them diligently day and night; one gives rise to a heart of compassion for all sentient beings; one gathers those without faith by generating pure faith; one gathers those who violate the precepts by upholding pure morality; and one always delights in benefiting others in all circumstances. This is what is meant by being subsumed under the beneficial conduct of one who cultivates the Mahāyāna.
What is meant by "common purpose" (*samānārthatā*)? It is as follows:

in all matters, one first acts in common with others, and then, through skillful means, instructs them to be diligent and firm in their pursuit of Bodhi. All wise ones should practice this Dharma in such a manner; practicing in this way constitutes the correct conduct cultivated by a Bodhisattva. If one is thus courageous and vigorous, they are called most excellent; having reached the other shore, they are fully able to penetrate the supreme Dharma-gate. This is what is called being subsumed under the "common purpose" of those who cultivate the Mahāyāna.
At that time, the brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Upon what do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas rely in order to be able to achieve the fruit of the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings?”
"How many kinds of abidings are there?
We pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will extensively expound all dharmas of abiding.
To speak in this way is equivalent to proclaiming the most supreme and marvelous gateway to bodhi."
The Buddha addressed the brahmin, saying:
"You should now know that there are three kinds of abiding.
They are as follows:"
The celestial abodes, the Brahma abodes, and the noble abodes.
Among these, what are called the celestial abodes?
They are as follows:
One should simply cultivate the practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

If a person first, toward the east, practices loving-kindness through the action of body, the action of speech, and the action of mind—vast and blazing—and likewise toward the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir, practicing loving-kindness through the action of body, the action of speech, and the action of mind, vast and blazing, this is called the "abode of the devas" (*devavihāra*).
What is called the Brahma-abodes?
They are the cultivation of the four immeasurable practices.
What are the four? They are loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; these are called the Brahma-abodes.
What is called the noble dwelling?
It refers to the cultivation of the three gates of liberation.
What are these three?
They are emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; these are called the noble abodes, and bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should dwell by relying upon such noble abodes.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The three abodes which I have taught Are the courageous and supreme Dharma;
For the sake of the assembly of bodhisattvas, I shall proclaim them according to what is appropriate."
If at all times one is able to act according to what has been taught,
I shall praise that person as one who seeks awakening.
This applies likewise to the celestial abodes, the Brahma abodes, and the noble abodes.
"Abiding within these three dwellings, one should settle accordingly;
if one dwells in this manner, one shall attain the state of non-extinction.
At that time, the brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the meaning of the Dharma-gate of Bodhi?
If there are sentient beings in future ages who ask me about this meaning, I will lack wisdom and be unable to penetrate all the Buddha-dharmas; how should I answer them at that time?”
“I pray that the Blessed One will explain this extensively for me.
Then the Blessed One spoke these verses for the brahmin:
“Brahmin, you should know: That which I have spoken for you;”
This vast and sublime Dharma exhorts the arousal of the bodhicitta;
through it, those who lack wisdom shall obtain it.
If one thoroughly understands this dharma-gate, that itself is the meaning of bodhi.
This Dharma that has been taught exhorts the arousal of the bodhicitta;
according to whatever beings inquire, it is able to reveal each and every point.
This Dharma that has been taught exhorts the arousal of the bodhicitta.
All wrong views and doubts can be severed;
in the final age of the Dharma's decline, if there is anyone who obtains this and holds the True Dharma in their hands, and that person practices giving—
That is to say, vast wealth and the like, Are the fulfillment of the practice of giving;
Through the accomplishment of giving, One reaches the further shore.
Furthermore, in the final age, If there be anyone who obtains this,
One who has received the True Dharma into their hands,
if they maintain the precepts with purity and without flaw, will then fulfill the practice of morality;
through the perfection of morality, they shall reach the further shore.
Furthermore, in the final age, if there is anyone who obtains this and the True Dharma falls into their hands, and that person practices patience,
calmly enduring all afflictions and disturbances, they will immediately fulfill the practice of patience.
Through the accomplishment of patience, one reaches the further shore.
Furthermore, in the final age, if there is someone who obtains this and the true Dharma falls into their hands,
and that person applies themselves with diligence, [they shall likewise attain liberation].
One who initiates with courage fulfills the practice of diligence;
through the accomplishment of diligence, one reaches the further shore.
Furthermore, in the final age, if there is anyone who attains this,
One who has received the True Dharma into their hands,
if they practice meditative concentration and abide in *samāhita*, will then fulfill the practice of concentration;
through the accomplishment of concentration, they shall reach the further shore.
Furthermore, in the final age, if there should be someone who obtains this and the True Dharma falls into their hands,
and that person cultivates wisdom and understands the most supreme Dharma, they will immediately perfect supreme wisdom.
By virtue of accomplishing wisdom, one reaches the further shore.
Furthermore, in the final age, if there should be someone who obtains this and the true Dharma falls into their hands, they will be able to honor and make offerings to it.
Know that such a person as this is called one who seeks bodhi;
they have drawn near to the Buddha’s bodhi and shall certainly achieve it.
Eighty koṭis of Buddhas empower this true Dharma.
If one obtains [this teaching] as it falls into their hands, they shall attain the supreme collection of dharmas.
If one hears this true Dharma in the presence of the present Buddhas,
know that such a person has thoroughly understood the meaning of a bodhisattva.
Those who love and delight in the Buddha’s bodhi—such people I know;
such people I see; I call to mind their names, and I, along with all the Buddhas, likewise praise them together.
If a person hears this Dharma and does not turn it to explain it to others,
they give rise to a mind of self-conceit and commit vast transgressions;
one should know that such persons do not respect the True Dharma.
At that time, the brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
You have well expounded this Dharma-gate; it is indeed the meaning of bodhi.”

If there are those who, in this present life, delight in understanding such meanings as these, they will before long attain great valor in this world; in future lives, they will skillfully expound the supreme Dharma, abide in Bodhi, and extensively bring great benefit to many beings.
The Buddha said:
"Brahmin! You have now been able to attain right wisdom and are able to speak such beneficial words."

"O Brahmin! If there are those who, having heard this Dharma before me now, are able to write down, uphold, read, and recite this True Dharma during the final age after my parinirvāṇa, you should know that such persons love and delight in the Noble Path and have resolved their minds upon Bodhi."

"Brahmin! In the past, when I was seeking awakening, I encountered a bhikṣu in a certain aranya who was proclaiming this Dharma. As soon as I heard this Dharma for a moment, I wept with tears of sorrow and reflected to myself:
'By what karmic obstruction in my previous lives did I not previously hear this true Dharma?'"
Having formed this thought, he immediately took a morsel of food and offered it to that bhikṣu, and then spoke again, saying:
"I do not understand the Dharma as I have heard it; I now wish to hear it, so I pray that you will explain it extensively for me."
"At that time, the bhikṣu explained it to me as was appropriate.
O Brahmin! Having heard this Dharma at that time, I immediately made this aspiration:"

“May I, in the future, through this True Dharma, provide empowerment and protective mindfulness within the final age, and extensively proclaim and expound it for the sake of all sentient beings. O Brahmin!
At that time, I further thought:
"When shall I be able to proclaim this True Dharma to sentient beings as is appropriate?
In the future final age, few among the various classes of sentient beings will be able to take delight in it or practice it."
"Later, at various times, when this Dharma remains in the world but no Buddha is manifest before me, I feel profound compassion for such matters.
O Brahmin! While I was reflecting in this way, there was a Buddha named Immeasurable Light who spoke these words:"
“Brahmin, it is through the power of aspiration that the fruit of retribution is accomplished. For this reason,
I take pity on all sentient beings who, shrouded in the darkness of ignorance, accumulate [karmic seeds] and undergo the terrors of saṃsāra.”

In the future final age, there will be certain bhikṣus who develop a sense of weary detachment toward this True Dharma; they will violate the prohibitions and precepts and become unvirtuous. For these reasons, they will be unable to propagate such True Dharma.
Therefore, O Brahmin! For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, I have extensively expounded this sutra.
You should know that this present True Dharma is a vast gateway to the teachings, which comprehensively subsumes the four Āgamas.
What are the four? They are:
the Saṃyukta Āgama, the Dīrgha Āgama, the Madhyama Āgama, and the Ekottara Āgama.

All such teachings collectively comprise the entire Śrāvaka-piṭaka; if any śrāvakas practice and study within them, they constitute the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, which is able to produce the fruits of the Śrāvaka-yāna and also encompasses the factors conducive to the enlightenment of a śrāvaka.

Furthermore, this sutra encompasses all the most supreme teachings of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; for this reason, it is named the Mother of All Dharmas. The entire Vinaya-piṭaka and Abhidharma-piṭaka are likewise subsumed within this sutra, and even the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (dharma-skandhas) each emerge from within this very sutra.

Furthermore, this Dharma of the sutra is the supreme root of the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), and it also gives rise to the wisdom of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; it is vast, profound, and inconceivable. It is a great radiance that universally illumines the three realms of existence (*trabhava*). This very [Dharma] arises from the root of all-knowledge as the bodhi of all Buddhas, encompassing all merits of giving, morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, and their most excellent liberation.
Such a treasury of manifold merits as these is all expounded in this sutra according to the truth.
Furthermore, the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—is likewise proclaimed within this sutra.
To state it briefly, this sutra summarizes:
all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, all dharmas are without self, and nirvana is tranquility.
For this reason, whether it be the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the Mahāyāna, these are explained in detail therein according to what is appropriate for each.
Furthermore, among all dharmas, this sutra extensively extols that bodhicitta; therefore, O Brahmin, this sutra is the most supreme and the most excellent.

If there are those who currently see the Buddhas and personally hear this Dharma, one should know that these persons have already heard the *Ratnavyūha-sūtra* from previous Buddhas and have already heard this Dharma within that sūtra. Therefore, one should know that the Dharma of this present sūtra has never been interrupted throughout the three periods of time, and various sentient beings have heard it according to their respective capacities.
At that time, the brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is rare, World-Honored One!

The Dharma taught by the Buddha is most supreme and profound. If ignorant sentient beings, upon hearing such a supreme true Dharma—the treasury of immeasurable merit—cannot give rise to a heart of deep love and joy, by what causes and conditions could such persons ever achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
Furthermore, World-Honored One,
for what cause and condition do many sentient beings give rise to doubt and confusion in their hearts regarding this most supreme Dharma of the Mahāyāna?
The Buddha said:

“Brahmin! You should know now that within this trichiliocosm, there are ten billion celestial palaces of Māra and ten billion Māra kings; each one has ten billion celestial Māra followers who constantly seek opportunities within this supreme Dharma-gate to create various obstacles, so as not to allow sentient beings to write, uphold, read, or recite it.”
Why is this? Within this trichiliocosm, there are many sentient beings who have attained the fruit of arhatship.

Yet, if among them there are sons or daughters of good family who, upon hearing this Mahāyāna Dharma-gate, resolve their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then when one weighs and compares their former merit against this resolve for bodhicitta, the former does not equal this resolve for bodhicitta.

Therefore, the celestial Māra seeks out difficult circumstances; because Māra creates these difficulties, many sentient beings, due to these causes and conditions, give rise to doubt and confusion in their minds. O Brāhmaṇa!
"Furthermore, this sutra is the king among all dharmas; for this reason, there are many obstacles.
At that time, the brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"
"By what skillful means can one cause all Māras to be naturally subdued?
The Buddha said, "Brāhmaṇa!"
I possess a secret dhāraṇī-dharmaparyāya called "Destroying Māras.
When I preach this dharmaparyāya, all Māras and their hosts shall be utterly destroyed.
"O Brāhmaṇa! Just as when the radiance of the sun's orb emerges and shines upon the world, all darkness and obscurity are completely eclipsed;
so too is this Dharma-gate for destroying Māra. When I preach it, the entire host of Māras is utterly destroyed."
At that time, the brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is this secret dhāraṇī, the Dharma-gate for destroying Māra?”
"I pray that the Buddha will explain it for me. The Buddha told the brahmin:
"You should listen attentively to the Dharma-gate for destroying Māra; its name is as follows:"

When the Blessed One spoke this secret dhāraṇī, the gate of the Dharma for destroying Māra, all the palaces of Māra shook violently; all the Māra kings and their hosts were utterly terrified and trembled, their hearts filled with anguish so that they could not sit at ease, and they all thought:

“The World-Honored One, out of compassion for all sentient beings, seeks their benefit and brings them peace and security; he benefits sentient beings through loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.”
"For what reason, at this time, do we, the various māras, fail to bring him benefit, but instead undergo such suffering and are unable to sit in peace?
"Furthermore, O brāhmaṇa!"

I now empower this Mahāyāna sūtra on the arousal of the bodhicitta with these secret dhāraṇī verses; thus, when this sūtra is preached in all places during the future degenerate age, no gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans shall find an opportunity to cause harm, and it shall be proclaimed, circulated, and spread without any obstacles.

If there are those who copy, uphold, read, or recite this True Dharma, such persons will remain far removed from all calamities, including those caused by kings, bandits, water, fire, insects, and beasts.
Why is this? This present True Dharma is the most supreme secret; out of compassion and for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, I proclaim it thus.

“Brahmin! The Buddha is never apart from loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity as he benefits sentient beings. If a son or daughter of good family practices according to reason as it has been taught, such a person shall attain virtuous conduct of the three karmas, extinguish all transgressions, and remain free from all suffering and affliction at all times.”
"Brāhmaṇa! For these reasons, you should know that this True Dharma can eliminate all suffering, extinguish all transgressions, destroy all Māras, and bring all dharmas to fulfillment."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Regarding those who cultivate goodness, Māra constantly watches for an opportunity;
desiring to incite various calamities, he seeks to destroy their wholesome dharmas."
If one hears this sutra being preached, even a single line or a single verse,
all those hosts of evil Māras will be completely subdued.
They will be struck with great terror and tremble, suffering in distress and unable to remain seated.
Due to the causes of those sinful karmas, such is the retribution obtained!
Because one constantly gave rise to a mind of affliction and harm toward all sentient beings,
and because one obstructed all wholesome dharmas, that cause and its effect do not fail.
If there are people who, regarding this Dharma, copy, uphold, read, and recite it;
such persons shall remain far removed from the perils of kings and the perils of bandits.
Perils such as water, fire, insects, and beasts—none of these various calamities shall be able to invade them.
Even humans and non-humans shall find no opportunity to harm them;
through virtuous conduct of body, speech, and mind, they sever all evil deeds;
at all times, they shall give rise to no suffering or affliction.
They remain far removed from all demonic activities and do not perceive any signs of demons;
they are also freed from all afflictions by virtue of upholding this sutra.
Having heard this sutra, they train themselves well according to what they have heard.
Skillfully understanding all phenomena, they advance toward the further shore.
Those who cultivate this Dharma penetrate the conduct of enlightenment;
having come by way of the path of enlightenment, they achieve perfect awakening.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the great Brahmin of the Kāśyapa clan, along with all the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and the world’s devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all filled with great joy; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
